facts.text: WASHINGTON — Under the Defense Department’s nearly $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 budget request, the Army would have almost $1 billion in procurement funding to spend on small counter unmanned aerial system technology (cUAS) capabilities — nearly double the amount the service was granted in its enacted budget for FY26.
This line also includes funding for logistics support efforts for small cUAS.
The largest chunk is for “operational” small cUAS capabilities at $414 million.
This includes broad funding for c-UAS batteries and “expeditionary” mobile platforms and sensors.
These include “dismounted, handheld, and wearable systems” for protection against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS threats, per the books.

The uptick in small counter-drone funding comes as the world continues to see inexpensive, small first-person-view drones taking out muti-million-dollar tanks on the modern battlefield, such as in the Ukraine-Russia war .
Separately, Honeywell Aerospace announced Oct.
12 that its wholly owned subsidiary, EMS Defense Technologies, was selected for a Department of Homeland Security counter-drone contract vehicle .
The five-year, multiple-award vehicle has a $1.5 billion ceiling, was awarded July 31 and took effect Aug.

Konicki said the interface is designed to be straightforward for operators, including younger service members who may be assigned counter-drone duties without extensive experience operating the different systems.
He said Honeywell Aerospace has demonstrated the software to U.S. government and military representatives, as well as local law enforcement and state and city representatives.
Counter-drone systems can combine radar, cameras, radio-frequency sensors and other equipment to detect, track and identify potential threats.
“There is no one solution that solves every threat out there,” said retired Air Force Col.
Tom Konicki, director of business at Honeywell Aerospace.
At the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting, Honeywell Aerospace displayed a mockup of the mobile configuration mounted on the back of a Ford F-150.
Honeywell Aerospace is also developing an airborne application of SAMURAI with Odys Aviation.
Announced in March 2026, the collaboration aims to adapt the system for Odys’ long-range Laila uncrewed aircraft.
The companies said the effort builds on more than a year of joint development and systems-integration work.
Customers can choose equipment suited to their needs and update components as detection technologies and countermeasures evolve.
He said the company seeks equipment mature enough for operational use rather than untested technology.
Electro-optical and infrared cameras allow operators to examine objects more closely, while acoustic sensors can help detect drones by their sound.
The company can then conduct what Konicki described as a red-team assessment, examining where an adversary might launch a drone and how that approach could affect the site’s defenses.
“There could be seven different sensors that have identified it and are feeding that into our software.”
